prompt: Which level of the hierarchy does every resource belong to directly?
hint: A topic has exactly one of them in its name.

choices.text: A folder, which may sit inside another folder
choices.why: Folders hold projects, not resources. A topic cannot be created in a folder.

choices.text: A project
choices.why: Right. Every resource lives in exactly one project, and the project's id begins its name.

choices.text: The organisation, through its domain
choices.why: The organisation is the root of the tree, several levels above any resource.

choices.text: The billing account that pays for it
choices.why: A billing account is linked to projects, and sits outside the tree altogether.

prompt: A role is granted on the folder `non-production`. Where is it held?

choices.text: On the folder only, until each project grants it again
choices.why: Inheritance is automatic; no project has to repeat a grant made above it.

choices.text: On the whole organisation, since folders share one policy
choices.why: Grants flow down, never up or sideways. `production` and the organisation are untouched.

choices.text: On the projects only, since a folder holds no resources
choices.why: The grant is held on the folder itself too, which is what lets somebody create projects in it.

choices.text: On the folder and everything below it
choices.why: Right. An allow policy is inherited by everything below the node it is written on.

prompt: Two projects sit in the same folder. What do they necessarily share?
hint: Think of what is inherited and what is linked.

choices.text: The policies inherited from the folder and above
choices.why: Right. They inherit the same grants and guardrails, and nothing else is shared by being neighbours.

choices.text: A billing account
choices.why: Billing is linked per project. Two neighbours may be paid for by different accounts.

choices.text: A network, because the folder is the network boundary
choices.why: A network belongs to a project. Sharing one across projects is a deliberate step, lesson 18.

choices.text: Their quotas, which the folder pools
choices.why: Quotas are counted per project; a folder pools none of them.

prompt: A freelancer opened Google Cloud with a personal Gmail address and built a client's system in five projects. The client hires a team and the freelancer leaves. What is the client's problem?
hint: What sits above the projects of a personal account?

choices.text: The projects are deleted when the Gmail account is closed
choices.why: Nothing deletes them on that day. The trouble is that their only owner is gone, not the projects.

choices.text: Projects cannot be moved under an organisation once created
choices.why: They can be moved under one later. What the client lacks today is the organisation to move them to.

choices.text: The projects have one owner, and nothing above them
choices.why: Right. With no organisation, the owner is whoever created each project, and nothing is written once for all five.

choices.text: Folders were never created, so the projects have no ids
choices.why: A project has its id from the moment it exists, with or without a folder above it.

prompt: Folders nest inside each other up to ___ levels deep.
Match each level of the tree to what it is.

pairs.right: the company, tied to one domain
a group of projects or of folders
the boundary every resource lives in
the topic, network or machine itself

right_distractors: the account that pays the bill

prompt: Which of a project's three identifiers can be changed after creation?

choices.text: The project id
choices.why: The id is fixed at creation and is in the name of every resource.

choices.text: The project number
choices.why: Google assigns the number at creation, and it never changes.

choices.text: The project name
choices.why: Right. The name is a label for people; rename it freely.

choices.text: The id and the number, together
choices.why: Both are fixed for the project's life. Only the third one moves.

prompt: A team deletes the project `planner-test` and, a year later, tries to create a new project with the same id. What happens?
hint: A project id is unique across all of Google Cloud, for good.

choices.text: It is refused: a deleted project's id is never handed out again
choices.why: Right. The id stays taken after deletion, so the new project needs another one.

choices.text: It succeeds, and the old project number comes back with it
choices.why: The id is not released, and a number is never reused either.

choices.text: It succeeds, as ids are only unique among live projects
choices.why: Uniqueness covers deleted projects too. That is what makes an id safe to keep in old logs.

choices.text: It succeeds only inside the same folder as before
choices.why: The folder has nothing to do with it. The id is global and taken.

prompt: In the lab, `gcloud pubsub topics create orders --project planner-prod` succeeded though no project `planner-prod` exists anywhere you own. What does that say about the emulator?
hint: Google would check the project first.

choices.text: It created the project `planner-prod` first, on the fly
choices.why: The emulator answers Pub/Sub only. Creating a project is the Resource Manager's job, and nothing in the lab answers it.

choices.text: It wrote the topic into `planner-dev`, the default project
choices.why: The list for `planner-prod` shows the topic there. `--project` overrode the default for that command.

choices.text: It sent the request to Google, which accepted it
choices.why: The override points Pub/Sub at the emulator, and Google would have refused the placeholder.

choices.text: It keeps the naming of projects without checking that a project exists
choices.why: Right. The project is part of every name in the emulator, and nothing more: it knows no projects.

prompt: Where is the full resource name `//pubsub.googleapis.com/projects/planner-dev/topics/orders` used rather than the short one?
hint: The prefix names the service. When would the service need naming?

choices.text: In every `gcloud pubsub` command
choices.why: The Pub/Sub commands take the short name, or just `orders` with the project from a property.

choices.text: Where several APIs meet
choices.why: Right. Inside Pub/Sub the short name is enough; across services the name has to say whose it is.

choices.text: Only in the console's address bar
choices.why: The console's addresses use their own form. The full resource name is the one the APIs share.

choices.text: In the request path the emulator receives
choices.why: The request goes to the service's own address, so the path starts at `projects/`.

prompt: `curl` to the Resource Manager for `projects/planner-dev` answers 401 `CREDENTIALS_MISSING`. What has the caller learnt about the project?
hint: At what point was the request refused?

choices.text: Nothing: the request was refused before any project was looked up
choices.why: Right. An anonymous caller learns only that it must sign in, whatever the id.

choices.text: That `planner-dev` exists, since a missing one answers 404
choices.why: The 401 comes first, for every id. It says nothing about whether the project exists.

choices.text: That the project belongs to another organisation
choices.why: Ownership would be checked after authentication, and the request never got that far.

choices.text: That the project is in the lab, since the lab sent the request
choices.why: The request went to Google's real API. The lab holds no project at all.

prompt: Why does `hierarchy.tf` give each project `folder_id = google_folder.production.folder_id` rather than a number?
hint: Who chooses a folder's number, and when?

choices.text: Folder numbers are secret and may not be written in a file
choices.why: They are identifiers, not secrets. They simply cannot be known in advance.

choices.text: A reference makes the folder optional
choices.why: Nothing about it is optional: the project needs the folder, which is why the order matters.

choices.text: It is invented at creation, so nobody knows it yet
choices.why: Right. The reference tells Terraform to create the folder first and fill the number in afterwards.

choices.text: The provider refuses numbers in `folder_id`
choices.why: A number is accepted when the folder already exists. Here it does not exist yet.

prompt: What does `terraform plan` contact to produce its answer in the lab?
hint: The token is a placeholder, and the plan succeeded.

choices.text: Google's Resource Manager, with the placeholder token
choices.why: Google would have refused the placeholder, as it does every time. The plan asked nothing.

choices.text: Nobody: it checks the provider's schema locally
choices.why: Right. For resources that do not exist yet, a plan needs nothing from Google.

choices.text: The Pub/Sub emulator, which stores the plan
choices.why: The emulator answers Pub/Sub only and knows nothing of folders.

choices.text: The Terraform registry, which validates each resource
choices.why: The registry supplied the provider at `init`. Planning uses the downloaded copy.

prompt: The plan for `hierarchy.tf` says `8 to add`. Applied with a real token, what would decide whether the folders are created?
hint: A plan checks the description; who checks the caller?

choices.text: Nothing more: a plan that passes is guaranteed to apply
choices.why: A plan proves the files fit the schema. Policies, quotas and permissions are checked later.

choices.text: Whether `terraform validate` was run before the apply
choices.why: Validation is the same schema check, done again. It cannot see a permission.

choices.text: Whether the plan was saved with `-out`
choices.why: Saving a plan pins what is asked for; it does not change who may ask.

choices.text: A permission on the organisation, checked by Google
choices.why: Right. `resourcemanager.folderCreator` on the organisation is judged at the moment of the request, by Google, and no plan can see it.

prompt: `hierarchy.tf` declares three folders and five projects. How many resources does the plan say it would add?
Put the Terraform commands of this lesson in the order they have to run.
hint: Nothing can be checked before the provider is there.
trap: Running `validate` first is the slip: with no provider downloaded, there is no schema to check the files against.

prompt: A company wants every project in production to forbid service account keys, and wants new production projects to get the rule without anybody remembering. Where is the rule written?
hint: Where does something written once reach every project below?

choices.text: On each production project, as it is created
choices.why: That is exactly the remembering the company wants to avoid. A folder does it once.

choices.text: On the billing account that pays for production
choices.why: A billing account carries no policies for the projects it pays for.

choices.text: On the project `planner-network`, which every project uses
choices.why: A rule on one project stays in that project. Neighbours inherit nothing from it.

choices.text: On the folder `production`
choices.why: Right. A policy on the folder is inherited by every project in it, including the ones created next year.
